common_name: Paul's Glory Hosta (Classic Gold-Centered Blue-Margined Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Paul's Glory develops its brightest gold center with some morning sun and is notably more sun-tolerant than many gold hostas without losing color, though the blue margin holds its cast best in shade.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with a few hours of morning sun for the brightest gold color at the center of the leaves. Introduced in the 1980s and named the American Hosta Growers Association's Hosta of the Year for 1999, Paul's Glory bears large, thick, cupped leaves that open chartreuse and mature to a rich, glowing gold center edged in an irregular blue-green margin, one of the most widely grown and influential variegated hosta cultivars ever released. Near-white flowers appear on tall scapes above the foliage in summer. Its heavy leaf substance provides good resistance to slug damage, and its combination of striking color, vigor, and reliability has made it a parent to numerous later hosta introductions. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring as new growth emerges.
sources: American Hosta Growers Association — Hosta of the Year 1999

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Ice Dance spreads by rhizomes more assertively than many sedges, so give it room or plan to divide and control its spread in smaller beds.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and divide every few years if a spreading colony needs to be contained within its bed. Ice Dance is an evergreen to semi-evergreen sedge forming dense, arching clumps of glossy dark green leaf blades edged in a crisp white margin, providing structure and cool-toned color to the shade garden through fall, winter, and spring when many perennials have died back. Inconspicuous brownish flower spikes appear in spring but are not the plant's draw. Unlike many clump-forming sedges, Ice Dance spreads steadily by rhizomes to form a broad groundcover patch over a few seasons, making it useful for erosion control on shaded slopes or as a filler beneath trees and shrubs, though it should be sited with room to spread or divided periodically to keep it in bounds. Cut back tattered winter foliage in early spring before new growth begins.

common_name: All Gold Hakonechloa (Solid Gold Japanese Forest Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; All Gold colors most brightly with a little morning sun but scorches in hot afternoon sun, and it spreads slowly, so patience is needed for the clump to reach full size.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, which scorches the bright foliage. All Gold is a solid-colored selection of Japanese forest grass bearing slender, gracefully arching, entirely bright chartreuse-gold blades that form a soft, cascading mound, glowing especially brightly in dappled light. Unlike running bamboo-relatives, Hakonechloa is a slow-spreading, well-behaved clumping grass that never becomes invasive, making it a safe, elegant choice for edging a shaded path, spilling over a container, or planting beneath larger shrubs. Its fine texture and luminous color pair beautifully with dark-leafed heuchera, hosta, and ferns. Cut back dried foliage in late winter before new shoots emerge, and be patient, since Hakonechloa is slow to establish and may take two to three seasons to reach its full spread.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sugar and Spice forms a slowly spreading, non-invasive clump and benefits from consistent moisture, especially in warmer parts of its range.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, mulching with leaf litter to keep roots cool and evenly moist. Sugar and Spice is a foamflower cultivar with deeply cut, maple-like green leaves marked by a bold, dark burgundy-purple central blaze that intensifies in cooler weather, topped by fluffy spikes of pale pink to white star-shaped flowers in spring that give the plant its common name. It forms a dense, slowly spreading, non-aggressive clump ideal for the front of a shaded border, a woodland path edge, or massed as a groundcover beneath deciduous trees, and pairs well with heuchera, hosta, and ferns for season-long foliage contrast. Foliage often takes on additional reddish tones through fall and can remain semi-evergreen in milder climates.

common_name: Sea Heart Brunnera (Compact Silver-Leaved Siberian Bugloss)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sea Heart holds its silver leaf color best out of hot afternoon sun and benefits from consistent moisture through summer, especially in warmer parts of its range.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, keeping soil evenly moist through summer since foliage can wilt or scorch in dry conditions or hot sun. Sea Heart is a compact Siberian bugloss cultivar bearing bold, heart-shaped leaves almost entirely covered in shimmering silver with only thin green veining, creating one of the brightest all-silver effects available among shade perennials, topped by airy sprays of small, bright blue, forget-me-not-like flowers in early spring. Its dense, well-behaved clump stays smaller and tidier than many older brunnera cultivars, making it a good choice for a shaded rock garden, container, or front-of-border planting where its luminous foliage can light up a dim corner from spring through fall. Established clumps rarely need division and self-seed only sparingly compared to the plain species.
